A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ND-LoRA research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, stream-corruption experiments, and component and module ablations for ND-LoRA.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds empirical theory fitting, stream-routing evaluation, and LoRA rank/alpha sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: A.7 adds a prompt-feature router that selects the number of streams; the core ND-LoRA architecture remains intact. Section 3.2 replaces the documented RandK expression with an all-pairs unsquared Frobenius loss, but Figure 2 still displays the squared loss. Whether this reflects changed training of the retained models is unresolved.

E1.justification: Both versions use The Pile and the same English hallucination, knowledge and general-capability benchmarks, including NQ-swap. The added routing and sensitivity analyses reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: The main Qwen LoRA, ParScale and component-ablation comparators are retained. The new routing analysis explicitly compares learned stream selection with oracle selection and a fixed P=4 reference (Section 5.4, A.7). The alpha alternatives in A.8 are configuration controls.

E3.justification: The empirical diversity measure changes from spectral D_spec to a cosine-based index D. V2 adds a two-parameter theoretical fit, a router trained on 10 samples per task and evaluated on held-out samples, and rank R16–R128 controls comparing alpha/r=2 with alpha=32. These substantially expand evaluation procedures while retaining the main training and benchmark setup.

E4.justification: The existing corruption experiments and component/module ablations remain. V2 adds quantitative theory-to-data fitting (Section 2.4), tests whether prompt features predict useful stream counts (A.7), and examines LoRA capacity, alpha scaling and optimization confounds (A.8, Tables 10–11).

E5.justification: Tables 10–11 introduce per-benchmark ± uncertainty entries, without defining their interpretation or establishing additional repeated runs. Figure 1 retains an 80% bootstrap interval but drops v1's explicit 1,000-resampling count. Existing significance tests and corruption-study seed information are retained.

E6.justification: The main benchmark comparison and Appendix Tables 7–9 retain their scores. V2 adds routing performance of 96.8% of oracle, rank/alpha sweep results, and theoretical-fit results reported inconsistently as R²=0.943 and 0.962. Table 4 replaces diversity measurements, including ND-LoRA's 0.3755 with 0.4112 under the revised index; these are not same-metric performance gains. Appendix cost estimates also change.

T1.justification: V1's scalar signal/noise model, spectral diversity index and approximation-error term are replaced by vector representation noise, an output-error threshold event and cosine diversity. V2 introduces Lipschitz, norm-concentration, kurtosis and shared-readout assumptions and rewrites the correlation lemma and hallucination-bound proof. Theorem 2 receives a new uniqueness derivation for all positive gamma, replacing the earlier convexity argument.

C1.justification: The central fixed-budget diversity thesis and the 25.6% maximum/14.6% average reduction claims remain. V2 broadens the novelty positioning to first formal hallucination tail bounds for ensembled language models, foregrounds quantitative theoretical validation, removes 'Small' from the title, and presents production-model scaling as straightforward.

C2.justification: V2 adds a retrieval-versus-verifiability explanation for task-dependent stream counts and interprets rank/alpha stability as ruling out optimization confounds. It also expands the distinction between architectures suited to mean performance and tail reliability. Section 7 drops v1's explicit English-only and computational-scale limitations, replacing its deferred production-scale validation with a claim that scaling is straightforward.

D1.justification: V2 documents final-RMSNorm whitening and cosine measurement, router features, coefficients and prediction rounding, and alpha=32 for the retained baselines. It removes the conflicting design-layer-16 statement while retaining layer 20 and revises cost accounting in A.2. Most optimizer, hardware, token-budget and training-time information is carried over.

R1.justification: The research positioning is substantially rewritten around mean-error optimization versus hallucination tail risk. New references include Markowitz, Krogh and Vedelsby, Bonab and Can, and Vershynin; portions of the previous PEFT, MoE and scaling discussion disappear. ParScale becomes a more explicit theoretical as well as architectural foundation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, related work and discussion. It shortens the regularization description, moves experimental setup from Section 4.1 to A.5, and reorganizes the appendices. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 adds a theoretical curve and revises its axis and legend. The task-optimality table moves near the front as Table 1, Appendix Tables 7–9 are consolidated onto one page, and Tables 10–11 are added. Figures 2–3 and the overall visual format are largely retained.

improvement.justification: The central theoretical justification becomes substantially less sound. V1 uses a signed scalar signal for its Cantelli argument; v2 defines a nonnegative error norm but assumes it has zero mean in A.1.2, invalidating the new tail-bound derivation. A.1.1 also incorrectly asserts a cosine inequality that would require general linear readouts to preserve orthogonality. Useful routing and sensitivity analyses and a clearer Theorem 2 derivation do not offset these central regressions. Conflicting fit statistics and removal of explicit scope limitations further weaken the paper's reliability.
